A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, tables and appendices. Substantial revisions and reorganizations can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original field-sampling experiments, Burgers data-assimilation results and optimal-control feasibility success rates.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original sampling, assimilation and control experiments, plus additional PDE benchmarks, runtime measurements and parameter studies.

M1.justification: V1's SAL uses a joint-distribution KL objective and an independently noisy projection update for z. V3 replaces these with an x-marginal KL objective and a deterministic projected update incorporating the previous z; its main algorithm also changes the dual step to τ/ρ. Section 3.3 introduces the adapted splitting constraint Ax=z for latent sampling. CASAL is therefore more than a rename.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix C.5 adds Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes and 2D Poisson reconstruction experiments. Section 5.3 replaces the one-dimensional restoring-force control problem with planar quadrotor planning around multiple obstacles. Energy-constrained field generation and Burgers assimilation remain.

E2.justification: V3 reports penalty-guidance comparisons beyond v1's unconstrained/projected and primal-dual comparisons, explicitly implementing Zhang et al.'s splitting penalty, Carvalho et al.'s guidance and Zampini et al.'s latent projected control method (C.2–C.4). Figure 2 replaces the primal-dual label with penalty, although C.2 still lists primal-dual sampling. Assimilation figures also replace the unconstrained label with penalty while retaining discussion of unconstrained diffusion.

E3.justification: The replacement control experiment uses 10,000 rather than 1,000 samples and different obstacle sizes. New PDE protocols include 25 observations and ten-sample posterior averages for Darcy, and 10% observed points with 50 posterior samples for Poisson. Runtime measurements and 1,000-versus-5,000-step ablations introduce additional evaluation procedures; the main Burgers trajectory-count protocol is retained.

E4.justification: V1 contains illustrative exploration and assimilation examples but no systematic hyperparameter ablations. V3 C.7 compares constant, linear and logarithmic coupling schedules and tests dual-variable initialization across field generation and Burgers assimilation. C.6 adds computational-overhead analysis, and Figure 5 extends the existing circle example with CASAL.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregated sampling and trajectory outcomes and show shaded bands in Figure 3 without defining their statistical meaning. V3's additional tables continue point-estimate reporting; no new confidence-interval, significance-testing, seed-reporting or uncertainty-estimation practice is introduced.

E6.justification: V3 adds PDE accuracy and constraint-violation results, runtime measurements and sensitivity results in Tables 1–6. For example, Table 3 reports Poisson reconstruction errors of 5% for CASAL, 15% for projected diffusion and 14% for penalty. Control success results are replaced for the quadrotor task; these are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V1 provides duality and asymptotic-recovery arguments and leaves finite-time convergence to future work. V3 revises the relaxed formulation and adds an optimal-density characterization, relaxation-error bounds, Gaussian-affine mean consistency, a Lyapunov analysis and a stated O(log t/sqrt(t)) KL mixing bound under explicit assumptions. Appendix D substantially expands the mathematical arguments.

C1.justification: Training-free strict constraint enforcement remains central. V3 additionally claims explicit mixing rates, a first Lagrangian-duality framework for this sampling problem in probability-measure space, and latent/physical-space decoupling with computational advantages. These become prominent contributions in the abstract and conclusion, whereas v1 explicitly leaves finite-time analysis unresolved.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations of finite-coupling bias and dual correction, latent-space computational savings, and failures caused by excessively small or large constant coupling. Projection-cost concerns are qualified using measured overheads. Future-work discussion shifts from finite-time analysis toward natively time-dependent diffusion formulations and improved approximate projections.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents ten-mode latent Fourier representations, a coupling schedule from 2 to 20, task-specific coupling values, projection and penalty implementations, and Apple M1 timing hardware. It also supplies a second code repository. The MLP architecture, 200 training epochs and 1,000 diffusion steps were already documented in v1; added representation details alone do not establish a changed earlier implementation.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands discussion of guided diffusion, latent constraints and physically constrained generation, including Zhang et al., Zampini et al., DiffusionPDE and physics-constrained flow matching. It develops the distinction between smooth penalty guidance and nonsmooth hard constraints and strengthens its positioning around a novel duality framework, beyond v1's shorter constrained-Langevin and variable-splitting discussion.

P1.justification: V3 integrates v1's standalone variational/duality background into the method presentation and creates a separate non-asymptotic analysis section. Related work becomes thematic, experimental descriptions gain explicit constraint paragraphs, and appendices are extensively reordered and rewritten. Terminology changes from SAL to CASAL accompany substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V3 adds six numerical tables, redraws Figure 4 with planar-position axes and different obstacle sizes, and expands Figure 5 from one panel to three comparative panels. Algorithm boxes, figure legends and document typography are also substantially reformatted.

improvement.justification: V3 adds valuable PDE/control evaluations, runtime comparisons, ablations and implementation details missing from v1. However, v1 leaves finite-time analysis open, whereas v3 claims a mixing rate whose proof in D.104 applies mixture convexity to the different object defined in the corollary: the law of an averaged iterate. Appendix C.2 also specifies a mass penalty for the energy benchmark. These inconsistencies affect central new theoretical and comparison claims, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the broader evidence.
